name: North Dravidian
region: Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and West Bengal in eastern India; Brahui in Balochistan (Pakistan and Afghanistan)
defining_innovation: Proto-Dravidian *k became x before non-front vowels: *kaṇ 'eye' is Kurukh xann and Brahui xan, against Tamil kaṇ.

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.body:
North Dravidian includes Kurukh (Oraon) and Malto, spoken by Adivasi communities in the hills of eastern India, and **Brahui**, spoken by two to three million people in Balochistan, far to the west in Pakistan. All three changed `*k` to a fricative *x* before back vowels, so 'eye' is Kurukh *xann* and Brahui *xan*, against Tamil *kaṇ*. The same change happened, entirely independently, in the Ugric branch of Uralic.

Brahui has been heavily influenced by Balochi and other Iranian languages. Only a small share of its vocabulary is Dravidian, although its grammar and many basic words clearly are.

chapters.title: The Brahui Question
chapters.body: Why is a Dravidian language spoken in Balochistan? One view is that Brahui is a relic of a time when Dravidian languages were spoken across the northwest, perhaps even in the Indus Valley. The other, argued by Josef Elfenbein, is that the Brahui migrated there from central India, relatively recently, after 1000 CE. Their language lacks old Iranian loans that a long residence should have left, and it is close to Kurukh and Malto. The question matters because it is often cited in the Indus debate.

speakers.note: Kurukh has about 2 million speakers and Malto about 230,000; the 2023 census of Pakistan counted about 2.8 million Brahui speakers.

sources.citation: Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig (eds.). 2024. Ethnologue: Languages of the World. 27th ed. Dallas: SIL International.

turning_points.title: *k becomes x
turning_points.description: Before non-front vowels, `*k` becomes `x`: `*kaṇ` 'eye' → Kurukh *xann*, Brahui *xan*. It is the main sound change uniting the North Dravidian languages, and it parallels Ugric `*kala` → *xul* on the Uralic tree.
turning_points.notation: *k → x / _ non-front V (*kaṇ → Kurukh xann, Brahui xan)

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju. 2003. The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

turning_points.date: Before c. 1000 CE, or much earlier
turning_points.title: Brahui in Balochistan
turning_points.description: Brahui ends up in Balochistan, separated from Kurukh and Malto by 1,500 kilometres. Whether it is an ancient relic or a medieval migrant is disputed.

sources.citation: Elfenbein, Josef. 1987. A periplus of the 'Brahui problem'. Studia Iranica 16.

turning_points.title: Brahui among Balochi speakers
turning_points.description: Widespread bilingualism with Balochi, and contact with Persian, Pashto and Sindhi, replaces most Brahui vocabulary and much of its sound system, while the Dravidian grammatical core remains.

sources.citation: Elfenbein, Josef. 1987. A periplus of the 'Brahui problem'. Studia Iranica 16.

turning_points.title: A script for Kurukh
turning_points.description: Kurukh activists introduce Tolong Siki, a new script designed for the language, as an alternative to Devanagari, and it is taught in some community schools in Jharkhand.

sources.citation: Steever, Sanford B., ed. 2020. The Dravidian Languages, 2nd ed. London: Routledge.
